card.title: STIRLING Mk III
card.text: Deployment: Shuffle a CARPET BOMBING into your deck.
card.flavorText: The Short Stirling was the RAF’s first four-engine heavy bomber to enter service in WWII. Designed by Short Brothers to meet Air Ministry requirements, it carried a large bomb load and was praised by crews for its handling. Its main weakness was a low operational ceiling, caused partly by the restricted wingspan required in the original specification. This made it more vulnerable than later heavy bombers such as the Halifax and Lancaster. The Mk III variant appeared in 1943 and became the main improved version of the Stirling. It used more powerful Bristol Hercules VI or XVI engines, raising maximum speed from about 255 to 270 mph. It also replaced the earlier dorsal turret with a fully-glazed FN.50 turret like the one used on the Lancaster, giving the gunner better space and visibility. Later Mk III aircraft carried electronic aids and countermeasures, including H2S radar, Monica rear warning radar, Mandrel jamming equipment, and chaff for confusing German radar. A total of 2,371 Stirlings were built. By late 1943, the type was leaving front line bombing service, but many Mk III aircraft were converted for glider towing and airborne support.
